Host A is 10.0.1.5/24 and host B is 10.0.2.5/24 on the same physical switch. Can they talk directly without a router?
No, they are in different subnets, so traffic must go through a gateway
Yes, because both addresses start with 10.0, so they share one private network
Yes, because a switch routes between any two IP subnets
No, because 10.x addresses cannot be used on a switch at all
With a /24 mask the networks are 10.0.1.0 and 10.0.2.0. Each host sends traffic for another subnet to its default gateway.
Which DNS record type maps a hostname to an IPv4 address?
A
AAAA
MX
CNAME
A records hold IPv4 addresses, AAAA records hold IPv6 addresses, MX records name mail servers, and CNAME records alias one name to another.
A recursive resolver with an empty cache looks up www.example.com. In what order does it ask servers?
A root server, then a .com TLD server, then example.com's authoritative server
The example.com server, then a .com TLD server, then a root server
A .com TLD server, then a root server, then the local hosts file
The authoritative server only, because it already knows every domain on the internet
Each level refers the resolver to the next one down the hierarchy, until the authoritative server returns the record.
You changed a domain's A record to a new IP, but some users still reach the old server for a while. Why?
Resolvers cached the old record and keep it until its TTL expires
DNS changes only take effect after the domain is renewed
Browsers ignore A records and use the IP from the first visit
The old server keeps answering DNS queries for the domain
DNS answers are cached for their TTL. Lowering the TTL well before a migration shortens the time old answers survive.
A browser opens https://example.com over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 with no existing connection. In what order do these steps happen?
DNS lookup, TCP handshake, TLS handshake, then the HTTP request
TLS handshake, DNS lookup, TCP handshake, then the HTTP request
DNS lookup, HTTP request, then TCP and TLS handshakes together
TCP handshake, DNS lookup, HTTP request, then TLS handshake
The browser needs the IP first, then a TCP connection, then TLS on top of it to secure the channel before any HTTP data is sent.
After the TLS handshake completes, how is the bulk application data encrypted?
With symmetric session keys derived during the handshake
With the server's RSA private key for every record
With the client's public key for every record
With the certificate authority's signing key
Asymmetric cryptography is used to authenticate and agree on keys. Data is then encrypted with fast symmetric ciphers such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305.
Which feature of the TLS key exchange gives forward secrecy, so a later leak of the server's private key cannot decrypt past sessions?
Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE or ECDHE) key exchange
Static RSA key transport of the session key
A longer validity period on the certificate
Pinning the server certificate in the client
Ephemeral keys are discarded after each session, so they cannot be recovered from the long-term key. TLS 1.3 allows only ephemeral key exchanges.
Which TLS extension lets a server hosting many HTTPS domains on one IP address pick the right certificate?
Server Name Indication
Protocol negotiation (ALPN)
OCSP certificate stapling
TLS session tickets
The client sends the hostname in the ClientHello through SNI. ALPN negotiates the application protocol, such as h2, not the certificate.
What does NAT (more precisely, port address translation) on a typical home router do?
Maps many private addresses to the router's public IP, using port numbers to tell connections apart
Assigns each device in the home its own public IPv4 address taken from the internet provider's pool
Encrypts all traffic between home devices and the internet provider's network
Translates domain names into IP addresses for devices on the home network
The router rewrites source addresses and ports on the way out and keeps a table to send replies back to the right device.
Why can't a host on the internet start a new connection to a game server running on a laptop behind a home NAT router, without extra setup?
The router has no mapping for unsolicited inbound traffic, so port forwarding is needed
The laptop's private IP address is blocked by every internet backbone router
TCP connections can only be opened from inside a private network to outside
The NAT router encrypts inbound packets so the laptop cannot read them
NAT mappings are created by outbound traffic. A static port forwarding rule, or a technique such as UPnP or hole punching, is needed for inbound connections.
cybersecurity: What is the goal of threat modeling?
Identifying likely threats and weaknesses in a design so they are addressed early
Scanning running production servers for known software vulnerabilities on a schedule
Writing the signatures that antivirus tools use to detect known malware
Recovering data and systems after a breach has already happened
Threat modeling is a structured design-time activity that asks what can go wrong and how to mitigate it, before the system is attacked.
Which letter of the STRIDE threat model stands for a threat to integrity, where data is changed by an attacker?
T, for Tampering
S, for Spoofing
R, for Repudiation
D, for Denial of service
STRIDE is Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege. Tampering maps to the integrity property.
Which trio of properties is known as the CIA triad in information security?
Confidentiality, integrity and availability
Control, isolation and auditing
Cryptography, identity and authorization
Compliance, inspection and accountability
The CIA triad names the three core goals: keeping data secret, unmodified and accessible to authorized users.
What is the difference between a vulnerability scan and a penetration test?
A scan finds and lists known weaknesses; a pen test actively tries to exploit them
A scan is done by outside attackers; a pen test is done only by automated software tools
A scan tests web apps only; a pen test tests networks only
A scan requires source code; a pen test never needs any access
Scanners compare a system against databases of known issues. A penetration test goes further and attempts real exploitation to show impact.
An authenticated vulnerability scan is run with valid credentials rather than unauthenticated. What is the main benefit?
It sees installed software and patch levels, so it finds more issues more accurately
It avoids generating any network traffic that could be logged by the target
It can only be run from outside the organization's perimeter firewall, like a real attacker
It guarantees that every finding it reports is a confirmed, working exploit
Logging in lets the scanner inspect the host directly, giving far more accurate results than guessing from the outside.
What is an attack surface?
The sum of points where an attacker could try to enter or extract data
The full list of users who have administrator rights on a system or network
The physical area a data center occupies in a building
The total number of lines of code in an application
The attack surface includes open ports, endpoints, inputs, interfaces and dependencies. Reducing it means removing unnecessary exposure.
Which action reduces a server's attack surface?
Disabling unused services and closing ports that are not needed
Giving every service account administrator rights for convenience
Opening extra ports so monitoring tools can reach the server
Installing as many packages as possible in case they are needed
Each running service and open port is a potential entry point. Turning off what you do not need leaves attackers fewer options.
What is the core principle of zero-trust architecture?
Never trust by default; verify every request regardless of network location
Trust any device automatically once it is connected to the internal corporate network
Trust traffic that comes from inside the corporate firewall by default
Trust users permanently after a single successful login with a password
Zero trust assumes the network is hostile and requires continuous verification of identity, device and context for each access, inside or outside the perimeter.
Which idea is central to zero trust and opposite to the old castle-and-moat model?
There is no implicitly trusted internal network; every access is checked
A strong perimeter firewall makes internal checks unnecessary
Once inside the VPN, a user can reach any internal service freely without more checks
Only external traffic needs authentication and authorization
The castle-and-moat model trusted everything inside the perimeter. Zero trust removes that implicit trust and verifies each request.
What makes an authentication scheme count as multi-factor authentication (MFA)?
It combines at least two factor categories, such as something you know and something you have
It requires two different passwords that the user must type one after the other
It asks the same security question twice, once before and once after the password
It uses one very long and complex password instead of a short and simple one
The factor categories are knowledge, possession and inherence. Two items from the same category, like two passwords, are not multi-factor.
Which authentication factor is an example of something you are (inherence)?
A fingerprint scan
An authenticator app code
A hardware security key
A memorized PIN
A fingerprint is a biometric (inherence). An app code and a hardware key are possession factors, and a PIN is a knowledge factor.
Why are hardware security keys using FIDO2/WebAuthn considered strong against phishing?
The key signs a challenge bound to the site's origin, so a fake site cannot reuse it
The key displays a six digit code that the user types into whichever site asks
The key stores the user's password and types it in automatically on each login
The key sends a one-time login code to the user's phone by SMS message
WebAuthn ties the credential to the real origin. A phishing site has a different origin, so the signature it would receive is useless.
Why is SMS considered a weaker second factor than an authenticator app or hardware key?
SMS codes can be intercepted or stolen through SIM swapping
SMS codes expire too quickly for users to type them in time
SMS requires the user to install a separate application first
SMS codes are reused, so the same code works more than once
SIM swap attacks and SS7 weaknesses let attackers receive a victim's texts. App-based TOTP and hardware keys avoid relying on the phone network.
In access control, what does the principle of least privilege state?
Each user or process should have only the permissions needed for its task
Every user should have the same permissions to keep things simple
Administrators should share one account to reduce the number of logins
Permissions should be granted generously and removed only after a breach
Least privilege limits the damage a compromised account or buggy process can do, because it can touch only what it truly needs.
What is the usual order of a well-formed security policy document hierarchy, from highest to most detailed?
Policy, then standards, then procedures
Procedures, then standards, then policy
Standards, then policy, then procedures
Procedures, then policy, then standards
A policy states intent and requirements, standards make them specific and measurable, and procedures give step-by-step instructions.
What does defense in depth mean?
Using multiple layers of controls so that one failure does not breach the whole system
Relying on one very strong control, such as a perimeter firewall, for all of the protection
Encrypting data so strongly that no other controls are needed
Hiding the system's design so attackers cannot understand it
Layered controls (network, host, application, data and people) mean an attacker must get past several barriers, and a single weakness is not fatal.
Why should passwords be stored as salted hashes rather than encrypted?
Hashing is one-way, so a database leak does not reveal the original passwords
Encryption makes login checks too slow for a real service at scale
Hashing lets the server recover and email a user's forgotten password on request
Encrypted passwords cannot be compared with the input at login time
A one-way hash means there is no key to steal that reverses it. The salt makes each hash unique so precomputed (rainbow) tables do not work.
Which example best illustrates the human element in security, often the weakest link?
An employee enters credentials on a convincing phishing email link
A firewall blocks an unexpected inbound connection attempt
A server applies a security patch automatically overnight
A backup job copies data to an encrypted offsite store
Social engineering targets people, who can be tricked into revealing secrets or taking unsafe actions, bypassing technical controls.
What is the main difference between authentication and authorization?
Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do
Authentication decides what you may do; authorization proves who you are
Authentication encrypts data; authorization signs data
Authentication is for users; authorization is only for servers
You authenticate first to establish identity, then the system authorizes specific actions based on that identity's permissions.
In incident response, why is containment typically prioritized early, before full eradication?
To stop the attacker from spreading or causing more damage while you investigate
To avoid alerting the attacker that they have already been detected by the security team
To restore all systems to normal operation before gathering any evidence
To assign blame to a specific team or person as quickly as possible
Containment (isolating affected systems) limits the blast radius first. Eradication of the root cause and recovery follow once spread is under control.
penetration-testing: In the OWASP Top 10, which flaw lets an attacker send input that a database runs as part of a query?
SQL injection
Cross-site scripting
Command injection
Path traversal
SQL injection mixes attacker data into a query so it is executed as code. It is part of the broader Injection category in the OWASP Top 10.
Which defense most reliably prevents SQL injection?
Parameterized queries (prepared statements) that separate code from data
Escaping single quotes in user input with a backslash before building the query
Hiding database error messages and stack traces from the user
Blocking the words SELECT and UNION in all incoming request parameters
Parameterized queries send the SQL and the values separately, so input is always treated as data. Blacklisting keywords and escaping are easy to bypass.
What does a stored (persistent) XSS attack do?
Saves a malicious script on the server so it runs for other users who view it
Tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a forged request to the server
Reads files from the server's disk through a crafted path in the URL
Floods the server with requests until it stops responding to other users
Stored XSS persists the script (for example in a comment) and serves it to every viewer. Reflected XSS instead bounces a script back in a single response.
Which output handling best prevents most cross-site scripting (XSS)?
Context-aware output encoding when rendering user data in HTML
Converting all user input to uppercase letters before it is stored
Validating on the server that every form field is present and not empty
Serving the whole site only over HTTPS with a valid certificate
Encoding user data for the context where it appears (HTML, attribute, JavaScript) stops the browser from treating it as markup or script. HTTPS does not stop XSS.
How does a CSRF (cross-site request forgery) attack work?
It makes a logged-in victim's browser send an unwanted request using their cookies
It injects a malicious script that runs inside the victim's active browser session
It steals the server's TLS private key in order to impersonate the real site
It guesses the victim's account password with many rapid automated attempts
The victim's browser automatically attaches their session cookie to a request triggered by the attacker's page, so the server thinks the user made it.
Which defense is specifically designed to stop CSRF?
A per-request anti-CSRF token that attacker pages cannot read
Hashing all stored passwords with a strong, salted algorithm
Encoding all output on every page to prevent script injection
Rate limiting the number of login attempts per minute per user
A secret token tied to the session, or SameSite cookies, ensures the request came from the real site, which a cross-origin page cannot forge.
A banking app uses URLs like /account?id=1001, and changing the id to 1002 shows another user's account. Which OWASP issue is this?
Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR)
Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
IDOR, a form of broken access control, exposes an object by its identifier without checking that the user is allowed to access it.
Which fix addresses an IDOR vulnerability?
Check on the server that the logged-in user owns or may access the requested object
Replace the numeric id with a longer random id and change nothing else on the server
Hide the id parameter by sending it in a POST body instead of the URL
Add client-side JavaScript that disables editing of the id field
The real fix is a server-side authorization check per request. Obscuring the identifier alone does not stop a determined attacker.
What is the purpose of the reconnaissance (footprinting) phase of a penetration test?
Gathering information about the target to plan the attack
Deleting log files so the test leaves no trace
Escalating from a normal user to an administrator
Writing the final report and findings summary for the client
Recon collects domains, IPs, services, employees and technologies. It shapes which attacks to try next and is the first step of the methodology.
What is the difference between passive and active reconnaissance?
Passive recon avoids touching the target and uses public sources; active recon probes it
Passive recon scans open ports, while active recon only reads public records
Passive recon needs valid credentials, while active recon never needs them
Passive recon is always illegal, while active recon is always fully permitted by law
Passive recon (WHOIS, search engines, certificate transparency) avoids contacting the target. Active recon such as port scanning interacts with it and is more detectable.
Which nmap command performs a basic TCP SYN scan of a host?
nmap -sS 10.0.0.5
nmap -sD 10.0.0.5
nmap -sz 10.0.0.5
nmap -sB 10.0.0.5
The -sS flag runs a SYN (half-open) scan, a fast and relatively stealthy way to find open TCP ports. The other flags are not standard scan types.
What is privilege escalation?
Gaining higher permissions than those first obtained on a system
Moving laterally to a different host on the same internal network
Encrypting a victim's files and demanding a ransom
Flooding a server with traffic to take it offline
After an initial foothold, an attacker tries to go from a limited account to admin or root. Lateral movement, in contrast, is spreading to other machines.
What is the difference between vertical and horizontal privilege escalation?
Vertical gains higher privileges; horizontal accesses another account at the same level
Vertical moves to another host, while horizontal escalation stays on one host
Vertical escalation is network based, while horizontal needs physical access
Vertical escalation targets Linux hosts, while horizontal escalation targets Windows hosts
Vertical escalation raises the privilege level (user to admin). Horizontal escalation takes over a different peer account, such as another user's data.
In Metasploit, what is a payload?
The code that runs on the target after a vulnerability is exploited
The scanner module that lists all of the open ports on the target host
The final report that is generated at the very end of an engagement
The database that stores every exploit and module in the framework
An exploit opens the door, and the payload (such as a reverse shell or Meterpreter) is what executes on the target to give the attacker access.
In a Metasploit reverse shell, which direction does the connection go?
From the compromised target back to the attacker's listener
From the attacker to a listening port on the target
From the target to another host on the same subnet
From the attacker's database to the exploit module
A reverse shell has the target connect outward to the attacker, which often gets through firewalls and NAT that block inbound connections (a bind shell).
What is Meterpreter in the Metasploit framework?
An in-memory payload that gives an interactive session with many post-exploitation commands
A port scanner module that maps the whole target network before exploitation
A password cracking tool used for fast offline dictionary attacks against stolen password hashes
A web proxy that intercepts and lets you edit HTTP requests in the browser
Meterpreter runs in memory to stay stealthy and offers features like file transfer, privilege escalation and pivoting through one session.
In network packet analysis with Wireshark, what does a display filter such as http.request.method == "POST" do?
Shows only packets that match, without discarding the captured traffic
Stops capturing any packet that does not match the filter
Deletes all packets that do not match from the capture file
Blocks matching packets from reaching their destination
A display filter changes only what is shown. A capture filter, set before capturing, is what limits which packets are recorded.
Why can an attacker on the same network often read another device's traffic more easily with a hub than with a switch?
A hub repeats every frame to all ports, while a switch sends frames only to the right port
A hub encrypts all of the traffic, so the attacker must decrypt it with a key
A switch is designed to broadcast all of the traffic it receives out to every one of its ports
A hub assigns one and the same IP address to every single connected device
On a hub, all hosts see all frames, so a sniffer captures everything. On a switch, an attacker typically needs techniques such as ARP spoofing to intercept traffic.
Why should a penetration test begin only after a signed scope and authorization (rules of engagement)?
Testing systems without permission is illegal and the scope defines what is allowed
The scope document lists all of the passwords and accounts that the tester is going to need
A signed authorization makes the tester a permanent employee of the client
The rules of engagement guarantee that no system under test will ever crash
Written authorization distinguishes a legitimate test from an attack and sets the targets, timing, methods and limits everyone agreed to.
What is the main value of the reporting phase of a penetration test to the client?
It documents findings, their risk and clear remediation steps
It proves the tester can bypass every security control
It permanently removes the vulnerabilities that were found
It replaces the need for the client to patch anything
The report turns the engagement into actionable improvements by explaining each issue, its impact and how to fix it, prioritized by risk.
cryptography: Which statement describes symmetric encryption such as AES?
The same secret key is used to encrypt and to decrypt
A public key encrypts and a private key decrypts
A private key encrypts and the same private key verifies
No key is needed because the data is only hashed
Symmetric ciphers use one shared key for both directions, which makes them fast but requires a secure way to share the key.
Which key sizes are standardized for AES?
128, 192 and 256 bits
56, 112 and 168 bits
64, 128 and 160 bits
AES supports 128, 192 and 256 bit keys with a 128 bit block. 56 and 168 bits refer to DES and 3DES, and 1024/2048 bits are typical RSA key sizes.
Why is the AES ECB mode discouraged for encrypting data such as images?
Identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext blocks, leaking patterns
It uses a key that is too short to be secure against modern brute force
It can only encrypt data that is exactly one block long, so large images will not fit
It requires a new key for every block of plaintext, which is impractical
ECB encrypts each block independently, so repetition in the plaintext shows up in the ciphertext. Modes like CBC, CTR or GCM avoid this with an IV or counter.
Which AES mode provides both confidentiality and built-in integrity (authenticated encryption)?
GCM
ECB
CBC
CTR
GCM produces an authentication tag that detects tampering, so it is authenticated encryption. ECB, CBC and CTR provide confidentiality only and need a separate MAC.
In asymmetric encryption, to send a confidential message you encrypt it with which key?
The recipient's public key
The recipient's private key
The sender's public key
The sender's private key
Only the recipient's private key can decrypt what their public key encrypted, so anyone can send them a secret but only they can read it.
Why is ECC (elliptic curve cryptography) attractive compared with RSA?
It offers similar security with much smaller keys
It does not rely on any hard mathematical problem
It encrypts data faster than any symmetric cipher
It removes the need to keep a private key secret
A 256-bit ECC key is roughly as strong as a 3072-bit RSA key, so ECC saves space and computation, which matters on constrained devices.
In practice, why are large files usually not encrypted directly with RSA?
RSA is slow and limited to small inputs, so it wraps a symmetric key instead
RSA cannot encrypt binary data, only printable text characters
RSA keys change with every message, so encrypted files could never be decrypted later
RSA provides integrity but not confidentiality for large files
This hybrid approach uses RSA (or ECC) to protect a random AES key, then encrypts the bulk data with fast symmetric AES.
What output size does the SHA-256 hash function produce?
256 bits (32 bytes)
128 bits (16 bytes)
512 bits (64 bytes)
160 bits (20 bytes)
SHA-256 always produces a 256-bit digest regardless of input size. SHA-512 produces 512 bits and the older SHA-1 produces 160 bits.
Which property of a cryptographic hash function means it is infeasible to find two different inputs with the same output?
Collision resistance
Preimage resistance
Avalanche effect
Deterministic output
Collision resistance is why hashes can stand in for data in signatures and integrity checks. Preimage resistance is the related property of not inverting the hash.
Why should a general-purpose fast hash such as SHA-256 not be used directly to store user passwords?
It is too fast, so attackers can try billions of guesses per second
It produces a 256-bit digest, which is too short to store a password safely
It cannot hash strings that contain special characters
It is reversible, so the password can be recovered from it
Password hashing needs to be deliberately slow and memory-hard. Algorithms like bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2 add cost and salting to resist cracking.
What does a digital signature provide?
Authenticity and integrity: proof of who signed and that the data is unchanged
Confidentiality, so that only the recipient can read the data
Faster transmission by compressing the data before sending
Anonymity, so the signer's identity stays hidden from all other parties involved
A valid signature shows the data came from the holder of the private key and was not altered. It does not hide the contents.
How is a digital signature created in schemes such as RSA or ECDSA?
The signer hashes the message and signs the hash with their private key
The signer encrypts the whole message with the recipient's public key first
The signer hashes the message with a secret shared with the verifier
The signer appends a random number chosen by the verifier
Signing the hash is efficient and binds the signature to the content. Anyone can verify it with the signer's public key.
Which key is used to verify a digital signature?
The signer's public key
The signer's private key
The verifier's public key
A shared secret key
The public key verifies what the matching private key signed. The private key is kept secret and used only for signing.
What does non-repudiation mean in the context of digital signatures?
The signer cannot plausibly deny having signed the message later
The message cannot be read by anyone except the recipient
The message is guaranteed to arrive at its destination
Two parties can share a key without meeting in person
Because only the signer holds the private key, a valid signature is evidence they produced it, so they cannot credibly disclaim it.
What does a public key infrastructure (PKI) certificate bind together?
A public key and an identity, vouched for by a certificate authority
A password and a username that are stored by a login server
A symmetric key and the IP address of the server that uses it
A private key and the serial number of the hard disk that stores it on the server
A certificate is a signed statement linking an identity (such as a domain) to its public key, so relying parties can trust that key.
In PKI, why can a browser trust a website's certificate it has never seen before?
It is signed by a certificate authority in the browser's trusted root store
The website sends its private key so the browser can check it directly
The certificate contains the user's own password as proof of identity
The browser contacts the website owner by email to confirm the certificate is real
Trust chains from a built-in trusted root CA down through intermediates to the site certificate. The private key is never shared.
What is the purpose of a certificate revocation list (CRL) or OCSP in PKI?
To let clients learn that a certificate was revoked before it expires
To renew a certificate automatically with the CA when it is about to expire
To store the private keys of all issued certificates safely
To translate a domain name into the server's IP address
A key may be compromised before the certificate's expiry. CRLs and OCSP let relying parties check whether a certificate is still valid.
Why does a certificate authority sign a certificate using an intermediate CA rather than its root key directly?
To keep the root key offline and limit damage if an intermediate is compromised
To make issued certificates expire much faster than the long-lived root certificate
To let website owners issue their own certificates for free without checks
To avoid having to include the public key inside the issued certificate
The root's private key stays offline and protected. Intermediates do day-to-day signing and can be revoked without replacing the root.
A one-time pad offers perfect secrecy. Why is it rarely practical?
The key must be truly random, as long as the message, and never reused
It can only encrypt text, not images or any other form of binary data
It is easily broken by modern computers within a few seconds of effort
It requires a separate public and private key pair for each message sent
The requirements for a truly random key the size of all data, shared securely and used once, make it unworkable for most real systems.
What does a nonce or initialization vector (IV) do in encryption modes such as AES-CTR or AES-GCM?
It ensures that encrypting the same plaintext twice gives different ciphertext
It replaces the secret key so the key never has to be shared with anyone
It compresses the plaintext before it is encrypted so the ciphertext comes out shorter
It stores the authentication tag that is used to detect any tampering
A unique IV or nonce per encryption randomizes the output, which is why reusing a nonce with the same key in these modes is a serious weakness.
blockchain: What is a blockchain?
An append-only ledger of blocks, each linked to the previous by its hash
A relational database controlled by a single trusted company or government
A peer-to-peer file sharing network for large media files
A cloud service that stores encrypted backups for users
Each block references the prior block's hash, forming a tamper-evident chain that is typically replicated across many nodes.
Why is a distributed ledger described as tamper-evident?
Changing one block alters its hash and breaks every link after it
Only administrators are allowed to edit older blocks in the ledger
Each block is encrypted so that its contents cannot be read by anyone
The ledger is stored on a single secured server run by one operator
Because each block commits to the previous hash, editing old data invalidates all later blocks, which honest nodes would reject.
What problem do blockchain consensus mechanisms solve?
Agreeing on one valid ledger history among distributed, untrusting nodes
Compressing the ledger so that it uses less disk space on every node
Encrypting every transaction so that only its sender is able to read it later
Assigning human-readable names to wallet addresses across the network
In a decentralized network with no central authority, consensus rules decide which transactions and ordering everyone accepts.
In Proof of Work, what must a miner do to add a block?
Find a nonce so the block's hash meets a difficulty target, which takes much computation
Prove ownership of the largest number of coins in the whole network
Collect valid digital signatures from a clear majority of the network's users and full nodes
Be selected by a central scheduling server that decides the order of miners
Miners repeatedly hash the block with different nonces until the output is below the target. The work is hard to do but easy for others to verify.
How does Proof of Stake choose who proposes or validates the next block?
By selecting validators based on the amount of cryptocurrency they stake
By rewarding whichever validator solves a hard hashing puzzle the fastest
By always letting the oldest running node in the whole network decide alone
By holding an open vote among every wallet holder for each individual block
PoS ties block creation rights to staked value, often with slashing penalties for misbehavior, and uses far less energy than PoW.
What is a 51% attack on a Proof of Work blockchain?
One party controls most mining power and can reorder or reverse recent transactions
An attacker manages to guess 51% of all users' private keys at the same time using brute force
More than half of the full nodes go offline at once, which stops the chain
A software bug lets anyone mint 51% more coins than the protocol allows
With a majority of hash power, an attacker can out-mine the honest chain to double-spend by rewriting recent blocks. It cannot forge signatures or steal arbitrary coins.
Which main drawback of Proof of Work does Proof of Stake aim to reduce?
Its very high energy consumption
Its reliance on digital signatures
Its use of cryptographic hashing
Its storage of the ledger on many nodes
PoW spends large amounts of electricity on hashing. PoS replaces that competition with staked capital, cutting energy use dramatically.
Which cryptographic primitive links each block to the one before it?
A cryptographic hash of the previous block header
A symmetric AES key shared by all miners
A digital signature from a central authority
A timestamp issued by a trusted time server
Each block header includes the previous block's hash. Any change upstream changes that hash and is immediately detectable.
Why does changing a single old transaction require redoing the Proof of Work for many blocks?
The edit changes that block's hash, so every later block's reference becomes invalid
Each transaction is individually mined with its own separate difficulty puzzle and nonce
Miners store only the single latest block and must recompute all of the rest
The whole network re-encrypts the entire chain after any change is detected
Because blocks are chained by hash and secured by work, rewriting history means re-mining the altered block and all blocks after it faster than the honest chain.
What is a Merkle tree used for in a block?
Summarizing all transactions into one root hash for efficient verification
Encrypting all of the transactions so that only miners are able to read them
Ordering the transactions in the block by the fees that each user has paid
Storing the private keys of every wallet that takes part in the transactions
Transactions are hashed in pairs up to a single Merkle root in the block header, so any change to a transaction changes the root.
What does a Merkle proof let a lightweight client do?
Verify a transaction is in a block without downloading all transactions
Decrypt the contents of a transaction using the block's stored Merkle root
Recover a private key that was lost by reading it back from the Merkle tree
Create and add a brand new block without doing any Proof of Work at all
A Merkle proof is the small set of sibling hashes needed to recompute the root, so a client can confirm inclusion with the header alone.
What does block height refer to in a blockchain?
The number of blocks between a block and the genesis block
The amount of data stored in a single block
The number of transactions waiting to be confirmed
The physical number of mining machines in the network
Height counts position in the chain. The genesis block is height 0, and each new block increases the height by one.
What is the genesis block?
The first block of a blockchain, which has no previous block
The most recent block that was added to the end of the chain
A special block that stores the balances of all of the users
The block that holds the full source code of the whole network
The genesis block is hardcoded as the starting point. It is the only block with no predecessor hash.
In a peer-to-peer blockchain network, how does a new transaction reach the miners or validators?
Nodes broadcast it and relay it to their peers across the network
It is sent to one central server that forwards it on to all the miners
It is emailed directly to the operator of each mining pool
It is written to a shared cloud folder the miners read
Transactions and blocks propagate by gossip: each node validates and forwards them to its peers, with no central coordinator.
When two valid blocks are mined at nearly the same time in Proof of Work, how is the fork usually resolved?
Nodes follow the chain with the most accumulated work once a block extends one branch
A central authority steps in and deletes one of the two competing blocks
Both of the competing blocks are merged together into a single larger block by the nodes
The block that happens to have the lower hash value always wins instantly
Temporary forks happen, but nodes adopt the longest (heaviest) valid chain, so one branch wins and the other's blocks become orphaned.
Why is a transaction often considered safer after several confirmations rather than one?
More blocks on top make reversing it through a reorganization far harder
Each confirmation lowers the transaction fee that was paid
The network re-signs the transaction with each new block
Confirmations encrypt the transaction more strongly each time a block is added
A reorg would have to outpace all the work in the blocks built on top, so deeper transactions are exponentially harder to reverse.
What distinguishes a permissioned (private) blockchain from a public one like Bitcoin?
Only approved participants may validate or write to it
It does not use any cryptographic hashing at all
It stores its ledger on a single central server
It cannot process more than one transaction per day
Permissioned chains restrict who can run nodes or propose blocks, trading some decentralization for control and often higher throughput.
Why does a public blockchain use economic incentives such as block rewards and fees?
To motivate participants to spend resources securing and extending the chain
To hide the real-world identities of everyone who sends transactions on the chain
To guarantee that sending transactions stays completely free for all users
To let a central bank control the total money supply of the network
Rewards and fees pay miners or validators for their work or stake, aligning their incentive to behave honestly with the network's security.
What does immutability of a blockchain actually mean in practice?
Once data is deeply confirmed, it is extremely costly and unlikely to be changed
Confirmed data literally cannot be altered by any physical means at all
Confirmed data is deleted automatically after a fixed period of time passes by design
Only the original author of the data is ever able to edit it again later
Immutability is economic and probabilistic, not absolute: rewriting confirmed history would require overwhelming resources and is rejected by honest nodes.
Why is losing the private key to a blockchain wallet usually permanent?
There is no central authority that can reset or recover it
The key is stored only on the exchange's servers, not by the user
A new key is automatically generated each month
The network emails a backup key to every user
Control of funds is proven solely by the private key. With no central operator and no reset mechanism, a lost key means the funds are unspendable.
web3: In a blockchain wallet, what is the relationship between the private key and the public address?
The address is derived from the public key, which is derived from the private key
The private key is derived from the public address each time you log in
The address and the private key are two completely unrelated random strings of text
The private key is simply the hash of the matching public wallet address
A private key produces a public key, and the address is derived from that public key. The derivation is one-way, so the address cannot reveal the private key.
What is a seed phrase (mnemonic) in a crypto wallet?
A list of words that encodes the master secret used to derive the wallet's keys
A password that only unlocks the interface of the local wallet application
The public wallet address that you share with others to receive incoming funds
A full backup copy of the blockchain that is stored on the user's device
A BIP-39 mnemonic encodes the seed for a hierarchical deterministic wallet. Anyone with the phrase controls all derived keys, so it must stay secret.
Why should a wallet's private key or seed phrase never be entered on a website?
A legitimate dApp never needs it, and any site asking for it is a scam that can steal funds
Websites are technically unable to process more than twelve words at once
The private key will only work correctly inside the official mobile wallet app for that chain
Entering it on a website makes all of your later transactions cost much higher gas fees
Signing happens inside the wallet, which never exposes the key to sites. A page requesting your seed phrase or private key is phishing.
What does a JSON-RPC provider give a web3 application?
An endpoint to read blockchain data and submit transactions to a node
A place to store large files completely off of the blockchain itself
A private key custody service that holds keys for the user's accounts
A compiler that turns Solidity source code into runnable EVM bytecode
Providers such as a node's RPC URL expose methods like eth_call and eth_sendRawTransaction, which libraries use to talk to the chain.
In an Ethereum JSON-RPC call, what does the eth_call method do?
Executes a read-only contract call without creating a transaction
Sends ether from one account to another account directly on-chain
Deploys a brand new smart contract onto the blockchain network
Mines the very next block in the chain and returns its block hash
eth_call runs a function against the current state and returns the result without changing state or costing gas. State changes need a signed transaction.
In a browser dApp, what does window.ethereum usually refer to?
The injected provider from a wallet extension such as MetaMask
A built-in browser API that is defined by the HTML standard itself
A direct TCP socket to an Ethereum validator node on the network
The private key of the account that is currently connected
Wallet extensions inject an EIP-1193 provider at window.ethereum, which the dApp uses to request accounts and send signing requests.
What does signing a transaction with a private key accomplish?
It proves the transaction was authorized by the account owner without revealing the key
It encrypts the whole transaction so that only miners are able to read it
It pays the required gas fee for the transaction directly out of the private key's own balance
It permanently deletes the private key afterwards as a built-in safety measure
The signature lets anyone verify, using the public key or address, that the account holder authorized the exact transaction, while the key stays secret.
On Ethereum, what is a nonce on an account transaction?
A per-account counter that orders transactions and prevents replay
A random value that is used to hide the identity of the sender
The gas price that the sender of the transaction is willing to pay
A hash of the smart contract that the transaction is calling into
Each account's transactions must use sequential nonces, so they execute in order and the same signed transaction cannot be replayed.
In ethers.js, what is the difference between a Provider and a Signer?
A Provider reads chain data; a Signer can sign and send transactions
A Provider signs transactions; a Signer only reads data
A Provider stores the private keys; a Signer only stores the public keys
They are the same object with two different names
A Provider is a read-only connection. A Signer holds or represents a key (often via a wallet) and is needed to authorize state-changing calls.
Using ethers.js, you have a read-only Contract and call a function that changes state. What happens?
It fails or only simulates, because sending the transaction needs a signer
It changes the state for free, because read operations never cost any gas
It first deploys a brand new copy of the whole contract before running
It automatically creates a fresh wallet in order to pay the transaction fee
State changes require a signed transaction, so the contract must be connected to a signer. A provider-only contract can perform read (view) calls.
What is the ABI (Application Binary Interface) of a smart contract?
A description of its functions and events that lets clients encode calls
The compiled bytecode of the contract that runs on the Ethereum virtual machine
The private key that is used to control all of the contract's funds
The physical network address of the node that happens to store it
The ABI is the schema libraries like ethers.js and web3.js use to encode arguments and decode results and events when interacting with a contract.
What is gas on Ethereum?
A unit measuring the computational work a transaction consumes
The native token that holders use to vote on protocol upgrades
A fee that is paid only when deploying a brand new contract
The time in seconds that a transaction waits in the mempool
Each operation costs gas, and the fee is gas used times the gas price, which compensates validators and limits resource use.
Why do wallets ask you to approve a token allowance before a dApp can move your ERC-20 tokens?
ERC-20 transfers by a third party require a prior approve of a spending allowance
Approving first converts the ERC-20 tokens into native ether automatically
The allowance encrypts the tokens so that the dApp is able to read them
Without an approval first, the tokens would simply be burned on any transfer attempt
The approve/transferFrom pattern lets a contract spend up to an approved amount. Granting unlimited allowances to untrusted contracts is a common risk.
In the ERC-20 token standard, what does the transferFrom function let an approved spender do?
Move tokens from an owner's balance up to the allowance the owner approved
Mint brand new tokens directly into the spender's own account balance
Transfer the owner's native ether out of the account instead of the tokens
Permanently freeze the owner's entire token balance so it cannot be moved
transferFrom works together with approve: the owner sets an allowance, and the spender (such as a DEX) moves tokens within that limit.
Which token standard is designed for non-fungible tokens (NFTs), where each token is unique?
ERC-721
ERC-20
ERC-777
ERC-721 defines unique tokens with distinct IDs. ERC-20 is for fungible tokens, and ERC-1155 is a multi-token standard for both fungible and non-fungible types.
Which standard is a multi-token contract that can manage both fungible and non-fungible tokens in one contract?
ERC-20
ERC-721
ERC-165
ERC-1155 supports many token types and batch transfers in a single contract. ERC-165 is a standard for detecting which interfaces a contract implements.
What is IPFS (InterPlanetary File System)?
A peer-to-peer system that addresses files by the hash of their content
A blockchain that is used to store all of the account balances for Ethereum
A centralized cloud provider that hosts files at one single fixed web URL
A protocol that is used for signing Ethereum transactions while fully offline
IPFS uses content addressing: a file's content identifier (CID) is derived from its hash, so the same content always has the same address.
Why is IPFS a popular choice for storing NFT metadata and images rather than a normal web server?
Content addressing means the data cannot be silently swapped, since the CID would change
IPFS automatically pays all of the storage costs on behalf of every user
IPFS guarantees that files stay online forever with no effort from anyone
IPFS encrypts all stored files so that only the owner's wallet is able to view or download them
A CID commits to exact content, so a token that points to a CID cannot have its image changed underneath it. IPFS does not guarantee permanence without pinning.
A file stored on IPFS stops being reachable over time. What is the most likely reason?
No node is pinning it, so it was garbage collected from caches
Its content identifier changed on its own
The Ethereum network deleted it after a year
The file expired because IPFS files have a fixed TTL
IPFS keeps content only while some node pins or caches it. Pinning services or your own node are needed to keep data available.
What does a smart contract being immutable after deployment usually imply for developers?
Bugs cannot be patched in place, so upgrade patterns or new deployments are needed
The balance held by the contract can never be changed by anyone at all
The contract automatically finds and fixes its own bugs as time goes on
Only the original deployer of the contract is ever able to call any of its public functions
Deployed bytecode normally cannot be edited, so teams plan for proxy-based upgrade patterns or redeploys, and audit carefully before launch.
